"Computational functionalism" is the philosophical position that Seth introduces here as the hidden load-bearing assumption behind every claim that AI could become conscious. As he defines it in this passage, the idea that consciousness is a matter of computation — more specifically, that implementing the right kind of computation, or information processing, is sufficient for consciousness to arise. His point in naming it is that people rarely notice they're making this assumption at all: this assumption... is so deeply ingrained that it can be difficult to recognize it as an assumption at all.

This term is the hinge the whole essay turns on. Everything that follows — the four arguments about brains not being Turing machines, about "other games in town" like analogue and dynamical systems, about life mattering, about simulation not being instantiation — is Seth's case for why this specific assumption is shaky. He's explicit that his stakes are high: if it's wrong, as I think it may be, then real artificial consciousness is fully off the table, at least for the kinds of AI we're familiar with.

It's worth distinguishing this from plain "functionalism" in philosophy of mind, a broader and older view — that mental properties depend on a system's functional organization, not on what it's made of — which Seth later notes is compatible with many non-computational theories too. Computational functionalism is the narrower, more specific claim that the relevant functional organization is *computational*, typically in the Turing-machine sense: that running the right algorithm, regardless of substrate, would be enough to produce experience. That narrower claim is what licenses ideas like mind-uploading, whole-brain simulation, and Bostrom's simulation hypothesis (all discussed later in the piece) — and it's precisely the claim Seth spends the rest of this section trying to undercut.

This is Seth naming the assumption he's about to spend the rest of the essay attacking. The sentence just before it lays out what the assumption actually is: the idea that consciousness is a matter of computation — more specifically, that implementing the right kind of computation, or information processing, is sufficient for consciousness to arise. In plain terms: if you build a system that processes information in the right pattern, consciousness just happens, regardless of what the system is physically made of. "Computational functionalism" is the philosophical label for this view — it's a real term used in philosophy of mind, not Seth's coinage, and it's the standard background assumption behind claims that a sufficiently advanced chatbot or a whole-brain simulation could be conscious.

The point of calling it "deeply ingrained" and hard to recognize "as an assumption at all" is to flag that most people arguing about AI consciousness aren't even aware they've adopted a contestable philosophical position — they treat it as simply obvious, almost invisible, the water they're swimming in. Seth's move here is to drag it into the light precisely so he can question it: And if it's wrong, as I think it may be, then real artificial consciousness is fully off the table, at least for the kinds of AI we're familiar with. Everything that follows in the essay — the "brains are not computers" argument, the material-substrate arguments, the biological-naturalism section — is Seth trying to show that this supposedly self-evident assumption is actually far from secure.

answers.asked: What does "computational functionalism" mean here, and why does it matter to the argument?
answers.text:
In the article, computational functionalism is the assumption that running the right kind of computation — the right information processing — is enough, by itself, to produce consciousness, no matter what the computation is running on. Seth writes that the very idea of conscious AI rests on the assumption that consciousness is a matter of computation — more specifically, that implementing the right kind of computation, or information processing, is sufficient for consciousness to arise, and he adds that this assumption is usually invisible: this assumption, which philosophers call computational functionalism, is so deeply ingrained that it can be difficult to recognize it as an assumption at all [spya-wepmnr].

It matters because Seth treats it as the single hinge the whole "conscious AI" idea turns on: if it's wrong, as I think it may be, then real artificial consciousness is fully off the table, at least for the kinds of AI we're familiar with [spya-wepmnr]. The rest of the essay's technical middle section — his four arguments that brains aren't computers, that there are "other games in town" besides Turing-style computation, that life itself may matter, and that simulation isn't instantiation — are all really different ways of attacking this one assumption [spya-cv97j7]. He makes the stakes explicit again in the summary: Computational functionalism — the claim that (algorithmic) computation is sufficient for consciousness — is a very strong assumption that looks increasingly shaky as the many and deep differences between brains and (standard digital) computers come into view [spya-ymbpwn].

He also uses it to catch other people's arguments assuming what they need to prove: he notes that whole-brain emulation and mind-uploading dreams "already assume" it [spya-pbcr03], and that Bostrom's simulation-hypothesis paper quietly relies on the same premise — that "a computer running a suitable program would be conscious" — without defending it [spya-xdy4fe]. So the term functions as Seth's diagnostic tool throughout: wherever someone claims or implies machines could be conscious, he traces the claim back to this one unexamined assumption and asks whether it actually holds.

Autopoiesis is a term coined in the 1970s by the Chilean biologists Humberto Maturana and Francisco Varela to describe what they saw as the defining feature of living systems: a living thing continuously builds and repairs its own components and maintains its own boundary (like a cell membrane), using its own processes, so that it keeps producing the very structure that produces it. It's a closed loop of self-manufacture — the system is both the product and the producer of itself, which is different from a machine, whose parts are made and assembled by something outside it.

In the passage, Seth uses it to make a point about neurons specifically: even a single neuron is "busy maintaining its own integrity and regenerating the conditions and material basis for its own continued existence," a process he calls autopoiesis, "from the Greek for 'self-production.'" He calls this "arguably a defining and distinctive characteristic of living systems."

The reason this matters for his argument is that it marks one of the deep differences between brains and computers he is building up in this section. A silicon chip just sits there running whatever program it's given; it doesn't have to constantly regenerate its own physical substrate to keep existing. A neuron does. So autopoiesis is offered as evidence that brain tissue isn't merely "hardware" running "software" — the biological material is doing something computers don't do at all, which feeds into his later claim that life itself, not just information-processing, may be necessary for consciousness.

answers.asked: (This process is called autopoiesis, from the Greek for “self-production.” Autopoiesis is arguably a defining and distinctive characteristic of living systems.)
answers.text:
Autopoiesis is a term from theoretical biology, originally coined by the Chilean biologists Humberto Maturana and Francisco Varela in the early 1970s, to describe how living systems continuously make and remake their own components and boundaries, rather than simply being built and then used, the way a machine is. A cell doesn't just run on its parts, it is constantly rebuilding those very parts out of the raw materials it takes in, so that the process of "doing" and the process of "being" become the same thing.

Seth introduces the word here as the technical label for something he's just described in plain terms: a single neuron is a spectacularly complicated biological machine, busy maintaining its own integrity and regenerating the conditions and material basis for its own continued existence, which he calls autopoiesis, from the Greek for "self-production." He adds that autopoiesis is arguably a defining and distinctive characteristic of living systems — meaning it's one of the things that marks the boundary between the living and the non-living.

This detail is doing real work in his larger argument. A few paragraphs earlier he argues that brains, unlike computers, have no clean separation between "mindware" and "wetware" — what a neuron does and what a neuron is are tangled together, unlike a computer where the software running is cleanly separable from the hardware it runs on. Autopoiesis is his concrete example of that tangling: a neuron isn't just executing a function, it's perpetually rebuilding itself in order to keep existing, which is exactly the kind of thing silicon components don't do. This is one plank in his broader case against "computational functionalism" (the assumption that the right computation is enough for consciousness) — if being alive in this self-producing sense turns out to matter for consciousness, then a computer simulation of a brain, however detailed, might never actually be conscious, since simulating self-production isn't the same as doing it.

answers.asked: What does "autopoiesis" mean here, and why does it matter to the argument?
answers.text:
In the article, autopoiesis is the self-producing, self-maintaining activity by which a living cell continually regenerates its own material conditions of existence — Seth even glosses the word itself: this process is called autopoiesis, from the Greek for "self-production," and Seth calls it arguably a defining and distinctive characteristic of living systems [spya-cf8rt8]. He introduces it while describing what makes a single neuron so much more than a simple signal-processing unit: even a single neuron is a spectacularly complicated biological machine, busy maintaining its own integrity and regenerating the conditions and material basis for its own continued existence [spya-cf8rt8].

Why it matters to the argument: it's one of Seth's main pieces of evidence that brains can't be cleanly split into "hardware" and "software" the way computers can. Because a neuron's very persistence depends on this self-producing activity, unlike computers, even computers running neural network algorithms, brains are the kinds of things for which it is difficult, and likely impossible, to separate what they do from what they are [spya-zw2m7u]. That separability is exactly what the "brain as computer" metaphor requires, so autopoiesis becomes a wedge against computational functionalism: the idea of the brain as a meat-based (universal) Turing machine rests precisely on this sharp separation of scales, on the substrate independence that motivated Turing's definition in the first place — if you cannot separate what brains do from what they are, the mathematical marriage of convenience starts to fall apart [spya-p4vmm0].

Later, autopoiesis resurfaces as the biological backbone of Seth's fourth argument, "Life Matters." He links the same self-regenerating property of cells to his predictive-processing account of consciousness: this drive to stay alive doesn't bottom out anywhere in particular — it reaches deep into the interior of each cell, into the molecular furnaces of metabolism, and within these whirls of metabolic activity, the ubiquitous process of prediction error minimization becomes inseparable from the materiality of life itself [spya-vys3vj]. So the concept does double duty in the piece: first as a reason brains resist the software/hardware split that makes Turing computation substrate-independent, and later as the biological ground on which Seth builds his tentative case that consciousness may require being alive, not just being computed [spya-cf8rt8 spya-p4vmm0 spya-vys3vj].
